extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, math students, educators, and authors selecting or evaluating elegant mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and operational rubric for choosing 'Book-quality' mathematical proofs — proofs that Aigner & Ziegler would include in Proofs from THE BOOK: accessible, illuminating, and aesthetically pleasing proofs suitable for undergraduate readers. Useful for editors, teachers, and evaluators of mathematical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Every proof must be intelligible to someone with basic undergraduate mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select proofs that do not presuppose advanced graduate-level background; aim for arguments a competent undergraduate reader can follow. This is a stated operational constraint by Aigner & Ziegler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-containment
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof should be readable without extensive prerequisite reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid proofs that require consulting many external results or long chains of prior theory. The proof should stand on its own within a short chapter or section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardy compatibility ('no ugly mathematics')
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject proofs that are 'ugly' — i.e., rely on brute force or inelegant calculations without conceptual clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aigner & Ziegler invoke Hardy's aesthetic standard: permanent ugliness disqualifies a proof from the Book. Prefer elegance and conceptual neatness over mere correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprising elementarity
rubrics_metrics.description: A deep result with an unexpectedly elementary proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Erdős's proof of Bertrand's postulate and proofs of the Cauchy–Davenport theorem. Favor proofs that reframe or demote hard results to simple ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of insight (one key idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof turns on one key idea that, once seen, illuminates the result completely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The key idea should be extractable and expressible succinctly; it should explain why the theorem is true rather than merely verifying it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof is short — it fits on a page or two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concision is valued because it allows the reader to grasp the whole argument at once. The Book favors arguments that can be presented in a single short chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: No machinery overkill
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using heavy tools when simpler ones suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce unnecessarily advanced frameworks or heavy formalism just to obtain a result that admits a lighter, more revealing argument (cf. 'Detlefsen–Arana purity' remark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: When existence is proved, the construction is explicit and natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer constructive proofs where the object in question is clearly exhibited or produced, rather than mere non-constructive existence arguments that hide the mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Book proofs admit a picture that captures the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric or diagrammatic proofs that can be visualized and whose picture encapsulates the idea are especially Book-worthy (e.g., many geometric proofs like Pick's theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-area significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The result (or its proof) matters beyond its native subfield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs whose ideas have relevance or applications in multiple parts of mathematics, indicating broader conceptual value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aha-moment
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader experiences a clear moment of 'of course!' when the key idea lands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Book-proof provides a satisfying cognitive 'aha' — the argument should reorganize the reader's perspective so the result feels inevitable once the idea is seen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization potential
rubrics_metrics.description: The technique extends to other problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book proofs often suggest natural generalizations or lead to a family of related results; prefer methods that are reusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-proof plurality
rubrics_metrics.description: When a theorem has many proofs, include the proof that exhibits the most distinct insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Book is pluralistic: it collects different proofs for the same theorem when each offers a different illuminating perspective (e.g., six proofs of the infinitude of primes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-trivial result
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof establishes a non-trivial mathematical result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book-quality proofs are not trivialities; they demonstrate interesting theorems whose proofs are not immediately obvious, even if the proofs are short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal machinery relative to depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses minimal machinery appropriate to the depth of the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the tools employed are the simplest that can reasonably obtain the theorem; unnecessary heavyweight frameworks that obscure the idea reduce Book-worthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprising reframing
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof reframes the problem radically, making a new viewpoint central (e.g., Fürstenberg's topological proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframing that reveals conceptual unity or shifts to a new domain (topology for number theory, etc.) is highly prized when it clarifies why a statement is true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short enough to grasp as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof is short enough that a reader can grasp it in one sitting (often 1–2 pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reiterates compactness but emphasizes pedagogical presentation: a chapter-sized exposition aimed at an undergraduate audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggests further work
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof suggests extensions or further research directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book proofs frequently point towards more general theorems or new problems; use this as a positive signal of conceptual richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns (proofs the Book rejects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of proofs excluded from the Book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: long combinatorial verifications without an organizing principle; proofs whose only virtue is formal correctness; proofs requiring heavy framework merely to state the result; proofs engineered only to fit a particular technique; proofs that obscure the key idea with technical apparatus. Use this list to screen out candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational checklist: Identify the key idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Can the key idea be stated in one sentence?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A primary evaluation step: if you cannot summarize the central insight succinctly, the proof likely lacks the singular illuminative quality the Book seeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational checklist: Evaluate machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the machinery minimal for the depth of the result?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the proof uses more advanced tools than necessary; minimal, revealing techniques score higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational checklist: Check for an aha-moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof produce an aha-moment in a competent reader?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a competent undergraduate experiences conceptual clarity upon seeing the key step; this subjective reaction is central to Book-quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational checklist: Fit-for-chapter
rubrics_metrics.description: Could the proof appear in a 1–2 page chapter of an undergraduate-accessible book?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical test combines compactness and accessibility; proofs that pass are strong candidates for inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational checklist: Extension potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof extend or suggest extensions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the technique generalizes; proofs that open avenues for more results are preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use as benchmark set for training evaluators
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Book's selected proofs as exemplars to train evaluators to recognize shared features of Book-quality proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aigner & Ziegler propose treating their selections as a benchmark set for comparative judgment and latent quality extraction; acknowledge Book-status is graded, not binary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality and subjectivity acknowledgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Book-worthiness is a partly subjective, pluralistic judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aigner & Ziegler explicitly note selections are their judgments and that other mathematicians would compile different Books; a rubric should treat Book-status as a graded aesthetic dimension rather than an absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples as supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonical examples illustrating the criteria (used as exemplars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited examples: six proofs of the infinitude of primes (plurality), Erdős's proof of Bertrand's postulate (surprising elementarity), Cantor's diagonal argument (one idea, total transparency), Fürstenberg's topological proof (radical reframing), Pick's theorem (geometric elegance + arithmetic surprise). Use these as positive exemplars when teaching the rubric.
